questions.q: Why was a single region, single provider, single vector database instance the RIGHT architecture for Northbeam's 100-user pilot, rather than a sign of an unfinished design?
options: A more elaborate architecture would have solved problems that didn't exist yet at that scale, at a cost not justified by 100 users
Simple architectures are always correct regardless of scale
The pilot architecture was actually wrong and should have included multi-region deployment from day one
100 users is too few for any architecture decision to matter at all
questions.explain: Matching architecture to actual current need, not a hypothetical future scale, is the core lesson here -- building Stage 4's complexity at Stage 1 would have been wasted effort solving problems that weren't real yet.

questions.q: At the 5,000-user Department Rollout stage, why was the fix 'entirely about discipline' (trimming a bloated prompt, setting budgets) rather than new infrastructure?
options: At that scale, cost and latency became real constraints for the first time, but the actual fix available was tightening what already existed, not building new infrastructure meant for a much larger future stage
New infrastructure is always required at every growth stage regardless of actual need
Discipline-based fixes are never sufficient at any stage of growth
5,000 users is identical in scale to 1,000,000 users for architectural purposes
questions.explain: The lesson is specifically that reaching for multi-region/multi-provider complexity at this stage would have solved a later stage's problem three stages too early -- the right-sized fix was prompt discipline and explicit budgets.

questions.q: At the 50,000-user Company-Wide stage, what specifically made capacity planning (Lesson 3) necessary for the first time?
options: The growth forecast showed the vector database tier would hit its ceiling in 7 months, and since the migration itself takes 3 months, the lead-time math -- not the raw ceiling date -- is what drove when the team needed to start
The team's existing infrastructure had already permanently failed by this point
Capacity planning was unnecessary at this stage and only became relevant at 1 million users
The forecast showed no growth at all, so no planning was needed
questions.explain: This directly reuses Lesson 3's lead-time point: the team started the 3-month migration at month 4 of a 7-month runway, giving comfortable margin instead of reacting to a capacity incident.

questions.q: Why did moving to a public-facing product at 1,000,000 users (Stage 4) specifically justify multi-region, multi-provider investment that would have been wasteful at Stage 1?
options: The risk profile changed -- an outage now meant real customer-facing downtime with reputational and revenue consequences, which justified the added cost of redundancy that an internal tool's occasional downtime did not
1,000,000 users is simply a bigger number, with no change in what an outage actually costs the business
Multi-region deployment is always correct at every stage regardless of audience
Public-facing products never experience outages regardless of architecture
questions.explain: The architectural change tracks a real change in business risk (internal inconvenience vs. customer-facing, revenue-affecting downtime), not just a bigger number of users on its own.

questions.q: What does the lesson say is the actual skill being tested by a 'how would you scale this system' interview question?
options: Knowing WHEN a sophisticated architecture choice is the right call and being able to explain why it would have been wrong at an earlier stage -- not simply describing the most advanced-sounding architecture
Reciting the single most robust possible architecture regardless of actual current scale
Listing as many distributed-systems buzzwords as possible in the answer
Describing only the final production architecture with no mention of how it got there
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly contrasts a staged answer (what changes and why, at each scale) against jumping straight to a maximally robust architecture -- the latter reads as inexperience, not expertise, to an interviewer or architecture reviewer.
